content.label: How to read this chapter
content.text:
Most chapters on a degenerative joint teach you to recognise the disease. This one is different, and it is worth saying why at the outset.

Acromioclavicular joint degeneration is close to universal with age. By the sixth decade most people have it on imaging, and most of them have no shoulder pain at all. So finding AC joint osteoarthritis on a scan tells you almost nothing about why your patient's shoulder hurts.

The skill this chapter teaches is therefore not recognition but attribution: deciding whether a degenerate joint that nearly everyone has is the joint actually generating this patient's pain. Get that wrong and you treat the wrong structure — or worse, send someone for an ablative operation that removes a piece of their skeleton for no benefit.

Everything below is organised around that single question.

content.label: Referencing
content.text: Each section ends with a short source line listing the references behind its figures. Full citations are in section 18. Where a figure reaches us through a review rather than the original paper, the originating author is named in the text and the review is credited in the source line.
Introduction, definition and terminology
What it is

content.body:
Acromioclavicular (AC) joint osteoarthritis is degenerative change of the small synovial joint between the lateral end of the clavicle and the medial border of the acromion — cartilage loss, subchondral change, marginal osteophyte formation and capsular thickening, in the same pattern as osteoarthritis anywhere else.

What distinguishes it clinically is not the pathology but the mismatch between how often it is present and how often it matters.

content.text: Primary versus secondary

rows: Previous AC injury or dislocation · distal clavicle fracture · repetitive heavy loading (distal clavicle osteolysis) · inflammatory arthropathy · septic arthritis · crystal arthropathy

content.body: In one surgical series of 56 patients, symptoms began at around 53–55 years and fewer than 50% reported any trauma.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: A symptomatic AC joint in someone under 40 is secondary until proven otherwise. Ask specifically about previous separation, a fall onto the point of the shoulder, and — above all — about bench press, dips and chest flies, because distal clavicle osteolysis in a lifter is a distinct condition with distinct management (section 5).
Terminology worth getting right

content.body:
• AC joint osteoarthritis — degenerative change involving both articular surfaces, with joint space narrowing and marginal osteophytes.
  • Distal clavicle osteolysis — inflammatory bone resorption of the clavicular side only, without osteophytes. A different disease, different population, different treatment.
  • AC joint separation — a traumatic ligamentous injury graded by the Rockwood classification. Can lead to secondary AC OA, but is a separate acute entity.

content.label: Pitfall
content.text: "AC joint arthrosis" on a radiology report is a description of anatomy, not a diagnosis. It becomes a diagnosis only when you have clinically localised the pain to that joint and, usually, confirmed it with an injection.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Surgical treatment review (PMC2684214); Radsource, distal clavicular osteolysis. Full citations in §18.
Epidemiology — and the attribution problem

content.body: This is the most important section in the chapter.

content.text: How common is it?

content.body: A systematic review of 10 studies and 1,831 shoulders in people not seeking care found:

content.text: And it rises steeply with age

content.body: Pooled cadaveric data by decade:
Individual imaging studies in asymptomatic people are starker still — all reported within the same review:

Four studies treating age as a continuous variable all found a significant association (pooled n = 765): Bonsell OR 1.080 per year (p < 0.001); Eriks-Hoogland adjusted OR 1.10 per year (p < 0.0001); Pennington Spearman's 0.65 (p < 0.01).

content.text: The number that should change your practice

content.body: A second systematic review of 31 studies compared imaging abnormalities in asymptomatic and symptomatic shoulders directly:

content.label: Key finding
content.text: AC joint OA was present in 13–95% of asymptomatic shoulders and 20–100% of symptomatic shoulders — ranges the authors described as "often comparable."

content.body: Across 21 non-population studies (1,794 shoulders, mean age 41), 27% had AC OA findings, with ranges of 6–47% on radiograph, 1–65% on ultrasound and 0–82% on MRI.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: Read that again. The prevalence of AC degeneration in people without shoulder pain substantially overlaps the prevalence in people with it. An abnormal AC joint on imaging therefore carries very little diagnostic weight on its own. Certainty was rated very low — all 31 studies carried a high risk of bias — but the direction is consistent across every study and every modality.
What follows from this

content.body: The authors of the prevalence review put it bluntly: AC joint OA is a common incidental finding and an uncommon cause of shoulder symptoms, so a radiographic finding has low pre-test odds of explaining the patient's pain. They recommend symptomatic AC OA be diagnosed sparingly, citing the twin risks of misattribution and harmful ablative surgery.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: The base rate is the whole problem. If 80% of 45-year-olds have AC degeneration on MRI, then finding it in your 45-year-old with shoulder pain is about as informative as finding that they have grey hair. The diagnosis has to be made on where the pain is and what reproduces it — and confirmed by response to injection — not on the scan.
Risk factors

rows: The dominant factor — OR ~1.08–1.10 per year
Separation or distal clavicle fracture → secondary OA
Less common, but changes management entirely

content.label: Sources
content.text: Prevalence review, people not seeking care (J Orthop), which also reports the Nicholson, Liou, Needell, Petersson, Eriks-Hoogland, Gumina, Bonsell and Pennington data; Imaging abnormalities in asymptomatic shoulders (J Orthop Surg Res 2024). Full citations in §18.
Relevant anatomy

content.body: Four facts, each explaining a clinical phenomenon.

content.text: It is small, flat and poorly congruent

content.body:
A plane synovial joint with a small contact area between the lateral clavicle and the medial acromion. The surfaces are relatively flat and incongruent, concentrating contact stress over a small area.

Why this matters: a joint with small contact area and high stress degenerates early and reliably. That is the anatomical reason the base-rate problem exists at all.

content.text: It contains a fibrocartilaginous disc that degenerates early

content.body:
An intra-articular disc sits within the joint and is frequently incomplete or substantially degenerate from early adulthood, well before symptoms appear in anyone.

Why this matters: "disc degeneration" on the MRI of a 30-year-old is a normal finding, not a lesion.

content.text: Two ligament systems, controlling two different directions

rows: Acromioclavicular ligaments (superior, inferior, anterior, posterior) — the superior is strongest

content.body: Why this matters enormously: the surgical treatment is resection of the distal clavicle. Resect too much, or damage the superior AC ligament, and you convert a painful stable joint into a painless unstable one — often more symptomatic. One series measured an average 5.5 mm increase in anteroposterior clavicular translation after resection (Blazar et al.). This single anatomical fact explains the commonest cause of a failed excision (section 15).

content.text: It transmits load and moves very little

content.body:
The joint transmits force from the upper limb to the axial skeleton via the clavicle. Its own motion is small — a few degrees of rotation and translation — with most apparent clavicular rotation during elevation occurring synchronously with scapular rotation.

Why this matters: the joint is loaded in compression during cross-body movement and in shear during overhead and behind-the-back movement. Those are precisely the positions that reproduce symptoms, and precisely the positions you modify in treatment.

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text: A small, incongruent, heavily loaded joint, stabilised horizontally by ligaments a surgeon must not damage. Degeneration is near-universal; instability after over-resection is iatrogenic and avoidable.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Standard reference anatomy, not drawn from a specific retrieved study. The Blazar translation figure and the provocative-position data are from the Surgical treatment review (PMC2684214).
Pathophysiology
The degenerative sequence

content.body:
1. Disc degeneration and fragmentation — early, largely asymptomatic
  2. Cartilage thinning and loss across both surfaces
  3. Subchondral sclerosis and cyst formation
  4. Marginal osteophyte formation, including inferior osteophytes projecting toward the subacromial space
  5. Capsular thickening and synovitis — the likely pain source in the symptomatic minority

content.text: Why most of it is painless

content.body: Nothing in steps 1–4 is intrinsically painful. Cartilage is aneural. The structures capable of generating pain are the capsule, synovium and subchondral bone, which is why symptoms correlate so poorly with radiographic severity, and why a joint can look destroyed and feel normal.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: The same lesson as glenohumeral OA, but more extreme: the imaging describes the structure; the examination and the injection describe the pain.
The inferior osteophyte and the impingement question

content.body:
Inferior AC osteophytes are often invoked as a cause of subacromial impingement. The evidence is weaker than the teaching suggests.

A retrospective MRI study (680 patients; 393 with confirmed subacromial impingement, 287 without) found no significant association between AC joint degeneration and impingement (p = 0.286), and none for acromion type III (p = 0.480). What was strongly associated was supraspinatus pathology — normal tendons in only 7.4% of impingement patients versus 32.4% of those without (p < 0.001) — together with a reduced acromiohumeral distance.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: Single-centre and retrospective, and it reports patient numbers inconsistently (608 in Methods, 680 in Results) — so it does not settle the question. But it argues against assuming an inferior osteophyte explains a patient's cuff-related pain, and against resecting the AC joint on that reasoning alone.
Coexistence — the real clinical problem

content.body:
Because AC degeneration is near-universal after middle age, it coexists with rotator cuff disease in most older patients with shoulder pain. The two are not alternatives on a differential; they are usually both present.

The clinical question is therefore not "is it the cuff or the AC joint?" but "how much of this patient's pain comes from each?" — a question the examination cannot answer reliably, as the next section shows.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Ahmad 2025 (Orthop Rev) for the impingement association data; Radsource, distal clavicular osteolysis, for the degenerative imaging pattern; Prevalence review (J Orthop) for the coexistence argument. Full citations in §18.
Distal clavicle osteolysis — a different mechanism
What it is

content.body: Painful inflammatory resorption of bone at the distal end of the clavicle, driven by repetitive microtrauma — or, less often, appearing weeks after acute trauma such as an AC dislocation. One proposed mechanism is chronic resorption during healing of a distal clavicle stress fracture, though this is debated.

content.text: Who gets it

content.body: Young adults, men more than women. Weightlifters above all — bench press, dips and chest flies — and also American footballers, gymnasts, rowers and workers doing repetitive pressing. Bilateral cases occur, itself a useful clue.

content.text: How to tell it apart from AC osteoarthritis

rows: Absent — isolated DCO does not produce them
Distal clavicular marrow oedema on fluid-sensitive sequences

content.body: Radiographs may be normal early. In the resorptive phase the distal clavicle appears thinned, with an indistinct or broken subchondral plate and erosions. MRI is the diagnostic modality and detects changes well before radiographs.

content.text: Management — and why it differs

content.body: Load is the cause, so load is the treatment. Stop or substantially restrict the provoking exercise; NSAIDs; corticosteroid injection if rest and medication fail; physiotherapy once the inflammatory phase settles.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: DCO is one of the few shoulder conditions where the history makes the diagnosis and the treatment is a conversation about training. A lifter with bilateral AC-region pain worst on bench press and dips has DCO until MRI says otherwise — and the intervention is to change the programme, not to inject the joint.

content.body: Natural history is favourable with load reduction, though radiographic recovery lags symptoms; in one reported case the joint appearance normalised about four years after symptoms resolved. Arthroscopic distal clavicle excision is effective for high-level athletes with persistent symptoms, with return to activity typically around six weeks.

content.label: Source
content.text: Radsource, distal clavicular osteolysis. Full citation in §18.
Clinical presentation
The typical story

content.body:
• Pain localised to the top of the shoulder, over the AC joint
  • Often pointed to with one finger — the most useful single historical feature
  • Worse on cross-body movement, on reaching behind the back, and on end-range overhead movement
  • Worse lying on that side
  • Worse on bench press, press-ups and dips in those who train

content.text: What argues against it

content.body:
• Pain referred to the deltoid insertion or down the arm
  • Night pain unrelated to position
  • Global restriction of passive movement — think adhesive capsulitis or glenohumeral OA
  • Pain in the mid-arc of elevation rather than the final degrees

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: The one-finger sign is worth more than most of the special tests. A patient who places a single fingertip precisely on the AC joint has meaningfully raised the probability; one who grasps the whole lateral deltoid has lowered it. The examination data below explain why that history matters so much.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Surgical treatment review (PMC2684214) for the provocative activities; Radsource for the lifting pattern. Full citations in §18.
Physical examination — and why the tests disappoint
The evidence base is thin

content.body: A systematic review found only two Level I studies of AC joint examination — Walton 2004 (n = 38) and Cadogan 2013 (n = 153) — and described a "paucity of high-level evidence." All figures below are from that review.

content.text: Individual test performance

content.label: Pitfall
content.text: Look at cross-body adduction. Its positive likelihood ratio is 0.86 — below 1. A positive test very slightly reduces the probability of AC pathology. The most widely taught AC joint test performs no better than a coin toss, and as a rule-in test it is worse than useless.

content.body: No single test has both acceptable sensitivity and specificity. O'Brien's is specific but misses 86% of cases; Paxinos is most sensitive but barely moves the probability.

content.text: Do combinations help? Marginally

content.body:
To rule in (both positive):

  • Paxinos + O'Brien's — specificity 0.96, sensitivity 0.11, LR+ 2.71
  • O'Brien's + AC tenderness — specificity 0.97, sensitivity 0.07, LR+ 2.08

To rule out (both negative):

  • Paxinos + Hawkins–Kennedy — sensitivity 0.94, LR− 0.35

Worked through: at a 40% pre-test probability, Paxinos + O'Brien's both positive raises it only to 64%; at 20% it reaches 40%, at 60% it reaches 80%. Both negative on Paxinos + Hawkins–Kennedy lowers a 40% probability to about 30%.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: The review's own conclusion: "Physical examination testing is not beneficial for diagnosis of AC joint pathology when pre-test probability is unequivocal" — in which case, proceed to procedural testing. The authors suggest ultrasound-guided AC injection may be an appropriate standard for both diagnosis and treatment.
So what should you actually do?

content.body:
Use the examination to screen out, not to confirm.

  1. Localise by palpation and by asking the patient to point.
  2. Use Paxinos + Hawkins–Kennedy as a screen — both negative makes AC pain unlikely (LR− 0.35).
  3. Reproduce the functional positions as a measure of impact, not as a diagnostic test.
  4. Examine the cuff and glenohumeral joint properly — coexistence is the rule.
  5. When it matters, inject.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: The examination narrows the field; the injection makes the diagnosis. An unusual thing to say about a musculoskeletal condition, and the direct consequence of a base rate near 100% and likelihood ratios near 1.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Krill et al. 2018, systematic review of AC joint physical examination (Phys Sportsmed), for all accuracy data; the two primary studies it analysed are Walton 2004 (JBJS Am) and Cadogan 2013 (BMC Musculoskelet Disord). Full citations in §18.
Differential diagnosis

rows: Lateral deltoid pain, mid-range painful arc, weakness on resisted testing, worse overhead than cross-body
Overlaps heavily; subacromial injection separates them
Loss of passive external rotation, crepitus, deeper posterior pain
Global loss of passive movement, especially external rotation
Younger, lifter, bilateral, marrow oedema without osteophytes
Trauma history, visible step, horizontal translation
Redness, swelling, fever, rapidly progressive pain — urgent
Bilateral, other joints, inflammatory history, effusion
Extends to trapezius and neck, worse with neck movement, normal local AC examination

content.label: Pitfall
content.text: Do not forget septic arthritis of the AC joint. Uncommon, easily dismissed as degenerative pain in an older patient, and a red, swollen, exquisitely tender joint with systemic features needs urgent aspiration, not an injection.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Surgical treatment review (PMC2684214) for the subacromial injection discrimination; Radsource for the osteolysis features. Remaining entries are clinical convention. Full citations in §18.
Investigations and imaging
Radiographs

content.body:
The Zanca view — AP of the AC joint with 10–15° cephalic tilt and reduced exposure. A standard shoulder AP overpenetrates the joint.

What you see: joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, marginal and inferior osteophytes.

What it means: remarkably little on its own — prevalence on radiograph in asymptomatic people ranges 6–47%.

content.text: MRI

content.body:
More sensitive, therefore less specific. Up to 80–90% of asymptomatic people over 40 have AC degenerative change on MRI; across studies the asymptomatic range is 0–82%. Its value here is in:

  • Detecting distal clavicle osteolysis (marrow oedema) — where MRI genuinely changes the diagnosis
  • Assessing the rotator cuff and coexisting pathology
  • Excluding alternatives

content.label: Pitfall
content.text: AC bone marrow oedema on MRI is reported as suggestive of a symptomatic joint, but its predictive value is modest. Do not treat it as confirmation.
Ultrasound

content.body: Visualises capsular distension, osteophytes and effusion; asymptomatic prevalence on ultrasound ranges 1–65%. Its real value is in guiding injection.

content.text: What imaging is actually for

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Image to exclude and to plan, not to confirm. Radiographs rule out other bony pathology and establish severity if surgery is considered. MRI identifies osteolysis and defines the cuff. Neither can tell you this joint is the pain generator — only the injection approaches that.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Prevalence review (J Orthop) and Imaging abnormalities in asymptomatic shoulders (J Orthop Surg Res 2024) for the prevalence ranges; Radsource for the osteolysis and degenerative imaging findings; StatPearls for ultrasound guidance. Full citations in §18.
Making the diagnosis — the diagnostic injection
How it works

content.body: Inject 0.5–2 mL of 1–2% lidocaine (or 0.5 mL of 0.25–0.5% bupivacaine) into the AC joint. The joint accommodates no more than about 2 mL — exceeding that guarantees extravasation into the subacromial space and destroys the test's specificity.

rows: AC joint is a meaningful pain generator
Look elsewhere — most often the rotator cuff
Mixed contribution — common, and important to recognise before surgery

content.text: The sequential injection

content.body: Where the picture is mixed, 5 mL of 1% lidocaine into the subacromial space on a separate occasion helps apportion the pain; persisting AC pain afterwards means the AC contribution is real.

content.text: Guided or landmark?

content.body: Landmark injections frequently miss, because the joint is small, obliquely oriented and variably angled. Ultrasound significantly improves accuracy and reduces complications and discomfort, and is increasingly preferred over fluoroscopy as non-invasive, cheaper and real-time.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: For a diagnostic injection, use ultrasound. A landmark injection that misses produces a false negative and may send a patient down an entirely wrong pathway. When the whole point of the procedure is the inference you draw from it, accuracy is not a refinement — it is the test.

content.label: Pitfall
content.text: A positive anaesthetic response is strong but not infallible. Volume spread, placebo response and partial contributions all limit it. Treat substantial relief as raising the probability, not as proof — particularly before recommending an irreversible operation.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Surgical treatment review (PMC2684214) for injectate volumes and the sequential injection; StatPearls, AC joint injection, for joint capacity and guidance accuracy. Full citations in §18.
Principles of treatment

content.body:
1. Confirm attribution before treating. With a near-universal base rate, the first therapeutic error is treating a joint that was never the problem.

2. Treat the load, not just the joint. Symptoms are reproduced by cross-body, behind-back and end-range overhead positions.

3. Treat the coexisting cuff. Most patients over 50 have cuff pathology as well.

4. Keep surgery genuinely last. At least six months of conservative management is the standard before considering distal clavicle excision; operative studies averaged 6 months of conservative care first.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: A 2024 systematic review of 48 studies and 1,902 shoulders (mean age 51, 58% male, mean follow-up 28.5 months) found the literature "did not establish that both non-operative and operative treatments are effective." Of those 48 studies, only one examined physiotherapy. Treat every recommendation below as reasonable practice with thin evidential support — and say so to your patients.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Treatment review 2024, 48 studies (PMID 38655415); Surgical treatment review (PMC2684214); Prevalence review (J Orthop). Full citations in §18.
Non-surgical management
Activity and load modification — the main intervention

rows: Reduce range (stop at chest level), reduce load, neutral-grip or machine variants
Re-sequence tasks; reach with the other arm
Lower the work height; use steps or platforms

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Most of the benefit lives here, and it takes a careful history to do well. "Avoid overhead activity" is not a prescription. "Stop your bench press at chest level and switch to a neutral-grip dumbbell press for six weeks" is.
Analgesia

content.body: Simple analgesia and NSAIDs, topical or oral, as a bridge enabling load modification and rehabilitation rather than as treatment in themselves.

content.text: Physiotherapy

content.body:
The evidence is close to absent — one study among 48. What is reasonable on mechanistic grounds:

  • Scapular control and posture, reducing time spent in provocative positions
  • Rotator cuff strengthening, addressing the usual coexisting pathology
  • Graded reintroduction of the provoking movement rather than permanent avoidance
  • Technique correction in lifters and manual workers

Avoid aggressive cross-body stretching into pain — it loads the joint in exactly the compressive direction that provokes symptoms.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Treatment review 2024 (PMID 38655415) for the physiotherapy evidence base; Surgical treatment review (PMC2684214) and Radsource for the provocative activities. The specific modifications are clinical reasoning, not trial evidence. Full citations in §18.
Rehabilitation programme

content.body: Progress on response, not on dates.

content.text: Phase 1 — Settle (weeks 0–3)

content.body:
• Identify and remove the provoking loads
  • Analgesia as required
  • Maintain full passive and active range — this joint does not stiffen if left alone
  • Scapular setting, postural work, cervical and thoracic mobility
  • Pain-free isometric cuff work in neutral

content.text: Phase 2 — Build (weeks 3–8)

content.body:
• Progressive cuff strengthening, avoiding end-range cross-body and behind-back positions
  • Scapular strengthening — serratus and lower trapezius
  • Begin loaded pressing in reduced range if relevant

content.text: Phase 3 — Reload (weeks 8+)

content.body:
• Reintroduce cross-body and overhead loading gradually, monitoring the 24-hour response
  • For lifters: restore range before restoring load, and correct technique
  • Address fear of reinjury explicitly in those who have stopped training

Dosing rule: pain ≤4/10 during, settling within 24 hours, no increase next morning.

content.label: Source
content.text: No published protocol exists for conservative AC joint rehabilitation. This programme is constructed from the mechanical principles in sections 3 and 12 and should be presented as reasoned practice, not evidence-based prescription.
Injections
What to expect — and the findings disagree

rows: Mean 50% improvement in pain at mean follow-up 7.5 months
Significant relief lasting at least 12 months after a single injection

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: Those findings do not agree, and you should not pretend otherwise when consenting a patient. Short-term studies up to three weeks are generally positive; mid- and long-term data are scarce and inconsistent. Repeated injections appear less effective, particularly in advanced degeneration.
Practical points

content.body:
• Volume: no more than 2 mL
  • Use ultrasound guidance
  • 25–27G needle
  • Combine with load modification — use the pain-free window to change the loading

content.text: What not to offer

content.body: Hyaluronic acid and PRP lack high-quality supporting evidence for this joint. Do not present them as established options.

content.text: Complications

content.body: Infection, bleeding, post-injection pain flare, skin and subcutaneous atrophy and hypopigmentation, tendon weakening, transient hyperglycaemia and systemic steroid effects.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Warn specifically about fat atrophy and skin depigmentation. Subcutaneous tissue is thin at the top of the shoulder, the change is permanent and visible, and patients who were not warned are reasonably upset by it.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Treatment review 2024 (PMID 38655415) for the pooled injection outcome; StatPearls, AC joint injection, for technique, complications, and the Hossain and van Riet figures it reports. Full citations in §18.
Surgical options
The operation

rows: Via subacromial space; requires bursectomy; preserves superior AC ligaments; combinable with acromioplasty or cuff repair

content.text: Outcomes

rows: 50–100% good results across series, averaging 76.3%; one series 72% good/satisfactory of 73 patients
54% excellent, 39% good, 7% poor — from continued distal clavicle instability
Mean functional outcome 87.8%; no significant difference open vs arthroscopic; 0.5–2 cm resection gave good outcomes

content.text: Why these operations fail — both causes preventable

content.body:
1. Diagnostic error. The AC joint was not the pain generator, or only partly responsible. This is the attribution problem arriving at its most expensive point.

2. Inadequate or excessive resection. Under-resection — especially of the posterior distal clavicle — leaves bony contact and persistent pain. Over-resection or superior AC ligament damage produces instability, with an average 5.5 mm increase in anteroposterior translation measured after resection (Blazar). Weakness is reported inconsistently; one series of 29 shoulders found none after indirect resection (Martin).

content.label: Pitfall
content.text: A patient worse after distal clavicle excision usually has one of two problems: the wrong diagnosis, or an unstable clavicle. Both present as persistent pain, but the unstable one often has a palpable clunk on cross-body movement. Examine for horizontal translation before assuming the operation simply "failed".
Post-operative rehabilitation

content.body:
• Sling for a few days only, for comfort
  • Assisted physiotherapy from 2–5 days
  • Range of motion as comfort allows — no repair to protect unless the cuff was addressed
  • Return to activity typically 2–3 months; around 6 weeks for arthroscopic excision in athletes with osteolysis

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Always read the operative note. If a cuff repair was done at the same time, that repair — not the clavicle — dictates the protocol.

content.label: Sources
content.text: Surgical treatment review (PMC2684214) for resection dimensions, outcome rates, complications and the post-operative protocol, including the Snyder, Zawadsky, Basmania, Blazar and Martin figures it reports; Treatment review 2024 (PMID 38655415) for the pooled comparison; Radsource for return to activity after excision in osteolysis. Full citations in §18.
Prognosis

content.body:
• Most AC degeneration never becomes symptomatic — around 50% of people not seeking care have it
  • Injection gives meaningful but variable relief — mean 50% pain improvement at 7.5 months, with wide spread
  • Surgery in correctly selected patients has good outcomes — ~76% after open, >90% in arthroscopic series, mean functional outcome 87.8% — but correct selection is the whole difficulty
  • Distal clavicle osteolysis has a good prognosis with load reduction, though radiographic recovery lags symptoms by years

content.label: Sources
content.text: Prevalence review (J Orthop); Treatment review 2024 (PMID 38655415); Surgical treatment review (PMC2684214); Radsource. Full citations in §18.
Key points

content.body:
1. The base rate is the diagnosis's biggest obstacle. Present in ~50% of people not seeking care, 70% of asymptomatic MRIs, and ~90% of asymptomatic people over 40. Asymptomatic prevalence (13–95%) overlaps symptomatic prevalence (20–100%).

2. Imaging cannot make this diagnosis. It excludes alternatives, identifies osteolysis and plans surgery.

3. The special tests are weak, and one is misleading. Cross-body adduction LR+ = 0.86. Use Paxinos + Hawkins–Kennedy to screen out (LR− 0.35).

4. Localisation plus a guided anaesthetic injection is the practical reference standard. Volume ≤2 mL, ultrasound-guided.

5. Coexistence with cuff disease is the rule after 50. Ask how much each contributes, not which one it is.

6. Under 40, think secondary — and ask about bench press. DCO is clavicular-side only, marrow oedema, no osteophytes.

7. Load modification is the main non-surgical treatment, and must be specific to the provoking movement.

8. Keep surgery last. Six months conservative first. The two causes of failure — wrong diagnosis and over-resection causing instability — are both avoidable.
